scenarios.title: Scenario 1 — Customer Support Resolution Agent
scenarios.domains: D1 Agentic Architecture · D2 Tool Design & MCP · D5 Context & Reliability
scenarios.brief: A retailer runs a tier-1 support agent on the Claude Agent SDK, handling about 12,000 tickets a week through four custom MCP tools: get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund and escalate_to_human. The agent may refund up to $500; larger refunds need human approval. Returns are accepted within 30 days of the order date. Orders come from three backend systems. First-contact resolution is 61% against an 80% target.

scenarios.title: Scenario 2 — Code Generation with Claude Code
scenarios.domains: D3 Claude Code Configuration & Workflows · D5 Context & Reliability · D4 Prompt Engineering
scenarios.brief: A 40-engineer platform team uses Claude Code in a monorepo with three trees: services/ (Go), web/ (React + TypeScript) and infra/ (Terraform). Each tree has its own conventions, and test files sit beside their sources. The root CLAUDE.md runs to about 900 lines. Engineers use Claude Code for generation, refactoring and exploration, and some keep personal setups alongside the shared configuration.

questions.question: A PreToolUse gate blocks process_refund until get_customer returns a verified customer ID. It went in after an audit traced a run of refunds to the wrong accounts. Guest-checkout orders, about 9% of volume, have no customer record, so every guest refund now escalates. Human agents clear these in under two minutes by matching the order email and the card's last four digits, and lookup_order already returns both values for guest orders. The support lead wants that queue gone this quarter. Which change best fits?

options.t: Exempt guest orders from the gate and add prompt steps, with two worked examples, for matching the order email and card last-four.
options.why: Runner-up. A clear written procedure with examples would be a reasonable way to add a second check if an occasional lapse were acceptable. This gate exists because an audit found refunds going to the wrong accounts, so the check has to stay in code.

options.t: Keep the gate as it is and attach a structured case summary to guest escalations so human agents can clear them faster.
options.why: Incorrect. A better handoff speeds the humans up, but every guest refund still escalates, so the queue does not go away.

options.t: Widen the gate's pass condition so a tool-confirmed match of order email and card last-four also unlocks that order's refund.
options.why: Correct. The gate stays deterministic but accepts a second proof of identity that the tools can confirm, so guest refunds can resolve on first contact without loosening control.

options.t: Have checkout create a lightweight customer record for each guest buyer so get_customer can return a verified ID.
options.why: Incorrect. A record built from checkout data proves nothing about who is in the chat, it changes another system, and it does nothing for guest orders already placed.

questions.explanation: When a prerequisite gate blocks a legitimate path, widen what the gate accepts rather than moving the check into the prompt. Identity checks before financial actions need programmatic enforcement, because prompt instructions have a non-zero failure rate.
questions.decider: The gate was added after an audit of refunds to the wrong accounts, so the guest check must be enforced in code; if an occasional lapse were tolerable, a prompt-based second path would do.

eli5.question: A code check blocks refunds until the customer is verified, but guest buyers have no account, so all their refunds go to humans. The clue is: the check went in after an audit found refunds going to the wrong accounts. So the question is how to let guests through without turning a hard rule into a polite request.
eli5.answer: Think of a bank door that only opens for a member card. Guests can't get in, so you add a second way in: the guard checks their order email and card digits. The door is still a door (a prerequisite gate in code); it just accepts two kinds of proof. Swapping the door for a sign saying "please check ID" would let some wrong people through. Rule: if a check must hold every time, widen the gate in code; don't replace it with instructions.
options: Runner-up. Written steps plus examples (prompt guidance) would do if an occasional slip were fine. After an audit of wrong-account refunds, it isn't.
A tidy handoff note helps the human, but every guest refund still goes to a human, so the queue stays.
Correct. The gate stays in code and accepts a second proof that the tools can check.
Making fake accounts at checkout changes another system and proves nothing about who is chatting now.

deep.premise: It is tempting to think the gate is the problem because it is what blocks guest refunds, so loosening it into a prompt instruction feels like the fix. The gate is not the problem; its pass condition is too narrow. You keep enforcement in code and teach the gate a second kind of proof.

questions.question: lookup_order fails in two ways: no order matches the ID, or the order database's read replica times out. Both return isError: true with the body "Operation failed". In about 4% of tickets the agent tells a customer their order does not exist when the lookup actually timed out, and several of those customers have since filed chargebacks. The timeouts cluster in evening peaks, and each episode lasts several minutes. Mistyped order IDs are common in chat. Which change most directly stops the false statements?

options.t: Retry the replica read inside lookup_order with exponential backoff, returning the error only once the retries are used up.
options.why: Runner-up. Local retry is the right first defence against brief blips and would win if each timeout lasted a second or two. These episodes last several minutes, so the retries run out and the agent still receives the same ambiguous failure.

options.t: Return an errorCategory of not_found or transient, an isRetryable flag and a short description the agent can relay.
options.why: Correct. Separate categories let the agent say an order is missing only when that is true, and treat a timeout as retryable, telling the customer to try again shortly.

options.t: Add a PostToolUse hook that rewrites the failure body into a message saying the order service is temporarily unavailable.
options.why: Incorrect. The hook sees the same "Operation failed" body in both cases, so it would tell customers with mistyped IDs that the service is down.

options.t: Instruct the agent in the system prompt to treat any failed lookup as a temporary outage and offer to escalate the ticket.
options.why: Incorrect. Treating every failure as an outage misleads the many customers who mistyped their order ID. The agent still cannot tell the two cases apart.

questions.explanation: A uniform error message stops the agent from choosing the right recovery. Structured errors that separate transient failures from a genuine not-found let the agent retry or explain accurately.
questions.decider: Each timeout episode lasts several minutes, so retries inside the tool run out and still return an ambiguous error; if timeouts were brief blips, local retry would be enough.

eli5.question: The order tool says "Operation failed" both when an order doesn't exist and when the database is slow. The agent guesses wrong and tells customers their order doesn't exist. The clue is: each slowdown lasts several minutes. So retrying quietly inside the tool won't be enough.
eli5.answer: Imagine a shop assistant who phones the stockroom. Sometimes nobody answers, sometimes the item truly isn't there, and both times the assistant hears the same beep. They will guess wrong. Give them two different answers: "not in stock" and "line busy, call back" (a structured error with an errorCategory and an isRetryable flag). Then they can tell the customer the truth. Rule: make the tool say what kind of failure happened, so the agent can choose what to do.
options: Runner-up. Quietly trying again (retry with backoff) fixes short blips. These outages last minutes, so the retries run out and the same vague error comes back.
Correct. Separate error types let the agent say "not found" only when it is true.
A rewrite step (PostToolUse hook) sees the same message for both cases, so it can't tell them apart either.
Calling every failure an outage misleads the many customers who just mistyped their order number.

deep.premise: It is tempting to think the timeouts are the problem, so the fix is to make them happen less. The real problem is that two different failures look identical to the agent. Even a rare timeout will still produce a false "your order doesn't exist" if the agent can't tell it from a genuine miss.

questions.question: Order dates arrive in three shapes depending on the backend: Unix epoch seconds, ISO 8601 with an offset, and a legacy integer such as 20260403. The agent decides whether an order is inside the 30-day return window. Audit shows eligibility is judged correctly for the first two systems but wrong about one time in nine for the legacy one, mostly near month ends. Tool-ordering instructions in this deployment are followed in roughly 95% of conversations. A fourth backend is due next quarter. Which TWO changes make the eligibility result independent of the source system?

options.t: Add a PostToolUse hook that converts every order date to one ISO 8601 form before the result reaches the model.
options.why: Correct. Normalising in code means the model never sees the legacy format, and the fourth backend needs only one more conversion rule in the hook.

options.t: Add a convert_date MCP tool and instruct the agent to call it before answering any return-window question.
options.why: Runner-up. A conversion tool takes the format work away from the model and would be a good pick if calls were reliably made. Instructions here are followed in about 95% of conversations, so roughly one answer in twenty would still skip it.

options.t: Add a system-prompt section documenting all three date formats with a worked conversion for each format.
options.why: Incorrect. Documentation leaves the conversion and the arithmetic to the model, which is where the month-end errors come from.

options.t: Have lookup_order return computed days_since_order and within_return_window fields with each order.
options.why: Correct. Computing the window in the tool removes the date arithmetic from the model entirely, so the answer no longer depends on the format.

options.t: Enable extended thinking for return-window questions so the model works the date arithmetic through step by step.
options.why: Incorrect. More reasoning may make errors rarer, but the outcome stays probabilistic and still depends on the format.

questions.explanation: Deterministic data handling belongs in code. Hooks normalise mixed formats before the model sees them, and tools can return derived values instead of asking the model to compute them.
questions.decider: Tool-ordering instructions are followed in about 95% of conversations, so a tool the agent must remember to call leaves some answers unconverted; if that call were enforced, convert_date would be a strong pick.

eli5.question: Dates come in three formats, and the agent gets the 30-day return check wrong for one of them. The clue is: written tool-ordering instructions are followed only about 95% of the time. So a fix that depends on the agent remembering an extra step will still miss some cases.
eli5.answer: Picture a post room where letters arrive in three languages. You can translate every letter before it reaches the desk (a PostToolUse hook that normalises dates). Or the sender can write "within return window: yes" on the envelope (a tool that returns computed fields). Either way, the clerk never does the risky translation. A dictionary the clerk is told to use helps only when the clerk remembers. Rule: if a result must not depend on the model, compute it in code before the model sees it.
options: Correct. Code converts every date to one format before the model reads it.
Runner-up. A conversion tool (convert_date) works when the agent calls it. It would win if that call were enforced, but instructions are followed only about 95% of the time here.
A cheat sheet in the system prompt still leaves the conversion and maths to the model.
Correct. The tool does the date maths and simply tells the agent the answer.
Thinking harder (extended thinking) makes mistakes rarer, not impossible.

deep.premise: It is tempting to think the model just needs better help with the legacy format: documentation, a converter, more thinking time. All of those still leave the model in charge of the step that fails. The question asks for a result that doesn't depend on the source system, which means taking the conversion and arithmetic out of the model's hands.

questions.question: A review of repeat contacts finds that 30% follow an opening message with several unrelated concerns, such as: 'the blender arrived cracked, I gave the wrong address for the order shipping Friday, and when does my filter subscription renew?' The agent settled the first item and ended its turn; the customer then wrote back about the rest. Each concern here typically takes one or two tool calls to settle, and the concerns rarely depend on one another. Which change most directly cuts these repeat contacts?

options.t: Spawn a subagent for each concern through the Task tool and have a coordinator merge their findings into one reply.
options.why: Runner-up. Parallel subagents suit concerns that each need a long, independent investigation whose output would crowd the main context. These take one or two tool calls each, so the coordination costs more than it saves.

options.t: Close every reply by asking the customer whether anything else in their message still needs attention.
options.why: Incorrect. The question keeps the door open but still ends the turn with work undone, so the customer has to come back. That is the repeat contact.

options.t: Check the draft reply for a mention of each concern before the loop accepts end_turn as the finish.
options.why: Incorrect. Matching words in the reply is an unreliable sign of completion. A reply can mention a concern without resolving it.

options.t: Have the agent list the distinct concerns at the start and work each to resolution or escalation before ending.
options.why: Correct. An explicit list of concerns gives the agent a checklist to finish within the same contact.

questions.explanation: Decompose a multi-concern request into distinct items and address each before ending the turn. Subagents earn their overhead when the work is heavy enough to need context isolation.
questions.decider: Each concern needs only one or two tool calls; if each needed a long investigation that would flood the context, per-concern subagents would be worth the overhead.

eli5.question: Customers raise three things in one message, and the agent answers only the first. The clue is: each concern needs just one or two tool calls. So the work is small, and the agent just needs to keep track of all of it. The question is not about running things in parallel.
eli5.answer: Think of a waiter taking a table's order. The fix is to write every dish on the pad and not leave until each one is served. You don't hire three extra waiters for three small dishes. Here the pad is an explicit list of concerns (decomposing a multi-concern request), and the agent works through it before ending its turn. Rule: list every concern first, finish each one, then end the turn.
options: Runner-up. One helper per concern (subagents via the Task tool) pays off when each concern is a long investigation. These take one or two lookups, so the coordination costs more than it saves.
Asking "anything else?" still ends the turn with work undone, so the customer has to come back.
Checking the reply for each concern's words is a poor finish signal. A reply can mention a concern without solving it.
Correct. A written list of concerns becomes a checklist the agent finishes in one contact.

deep.premise: It is tempting to think several independent concerns call for parallel subagents, because the stem stresses that they don't depend on one another. Independence makes parallel work possible; it doesn't make it worth it. Subagents earn their overhead when each job is heavy enough to flood the context. One or two tool calls each is not heavy.

questions.question: First-contact resolution is 61% against an 80% target. A labelled sample shows the agent escalates 22% of tickets that a human then closed with no policy exception, and attempts 6% that needed one, sometimes promising remedies the company does not offer. The system prompt's escalation guidance is a single sentence: 'escalate when appropriate.' An engineer proposes that the model output a confidence score each turn, with anything below 0.7 routed to a human. Which is the best evaluation of the proposal?

options.t: Adopt it, and calibrate the 0.7 cut-off against the labelled sample until both error rates reach their targets.
options.why: Incorrect. Calibrating on labelled data works for field-level scores in extraction, but the model's own rating does not track whether a ticket needs a policy exception. Moving the cut-off trades one error for the other.

options.t: Reject it, and write explicit escalate-versus-resolve criteria with a few contrasting tickets as examples.
options.why: Correct. The agent has almost no definition of when to escalate. Explicit criteria plus contrasting examples address both error directions at proportionate cost.

options.t: Reject it, and train a classifier on past escalation labels to route each ticket before the agent replies.
options.why: Runner-up. A trained classifier would be worth its cost if clear criteria and examples were already in place and still failing. Here the guidance is one vague sentence, so the cheaper fix comes first.

options.t: Adopt it, and add a sentiment check that escalates frustrated customers whatever score the model reports.
options.why: Incorrect. Sentiment does not track complexity. Calm customers can need exceptions, and angry ones often have simple problems.

questions.explanation: Self-reported confidence and sentiment are unreliable proxies for case complexity. When the escalation boundary is unclear, define it with explicit criteria and contrasting examples first.
questions.decider: The escalation guidance is one vague sentence, so explicit criteria and examples are the proportionate fix; if detailed criteria were already in place and failing, a trained classifier would come next.

eli5.question: The agent escalates easy tickets and tries to handle hard ones. Someone wants the model to rate its own confidence and escalate below 0.7. The clue is: the only escalation guidance today is one sentence, "escalate when appropriate". So the agent has never been told where the line is.
eli5.answer: Imagine a new employee whose only instruction is "ask your manager when appropriate". Asking them how sure they feel won't help; they don't know the rules, so their confidence means little. Write down when to ask and when not to, and show a few real cases (explicit criteria plus few-shot examples). A self-rating (self-reported confidence) does not track how complex a case really is. Rule: when the boundary is unclear, define it; don't measure the model's feelings about it.
options: Tuning the cut-off just trades one error for the other. The model's own score doesn't track whether a ticket needs a policy exception.
Correct. Clear escalate-versus-resolve rules plus contrasting examples fix both directions cheaply.
Runner-up. A trained classifier is worth its cost once clear rules exist and still fail. Here the rules are one vague sentence, so write them first.
Mood (sentiment) isn't complexity. Calm customers can need exceptions; angry ones often have simple problems.

deep.premise: It is tempting to think a number makes escalation measurable and tunable, so a confidence threshold, or a classifier, sounds rigorous. The model's self-rating is not tied to whether a case needs a policy exception. The cheaper, more direct cause is visible: the agent has almost no definition of when to escalate.

questions.question: Conversations average 34 turns. After about turn twenty the agent quotes refunds as $47.00 when the tool returned $47.99, asks again for an order number the customer typed long before, and refers to 'our usual returns policy' instead of the window it looked up. Each get_customer call returns 40-odd fields and is repeated several times per conversation. The errors begin while the context window is still under half full. Compliance requires every customer and agent turn to stay in the history verbatim. Which TWO changes best preserve the facts the resolution depends on?

options.t: Move the agent to a model with a larger context window and keep the full history in every request.
options.why: Runner-up. More room helps when history is being cut off. The errors start with the window under half full, so this is facts getting lost in the middle of a long, noisy history, not overflow.

options.t: Keep a case-facts block of IDs, exact amounts, policy dates and commitments at the top of each request.
options.why: Correct. Exact facts kept together at the start sit where the model reads most reliably, whatever happens in the middle of a long history.

options.t: Strip each tool result down to the handful of fields the workflow uses before it is added to the history.
options.why: Correct. Repeated 40-field results bury the few values that matter. Trimming them cuts the noise around the important facts.

options.t: Summarise the conversation every ten turns and replace the summarised turns with that summary in the history.
options.why: Incorrect. Compliance needs the turns kept verbatim, and progressive summaries tend to round amounts and blur dates.

options.t: Call get_customer and lookup_order again before each reply to give the agent fresh values.
options.why: Incorrect. Re-fetching adds even more verbose results, and it cannot recover the order number the customer typed.

questions.explanation: Keep transactional facts in a persistent case-facts block at the start of the context and trim verbose tool output to the fields that matter. Bigger windows do not fix the lost-in-the-middle effect.
questions.decider: The errors begin with the context under half full, so the problem is facts lost in a noisy middle, not lack of room; if the history were overflowing, a larger window would be a strong candidate.

eli5.question: In long chats the agent gets amounts wrong and forgets things the customer said. The clue is: the errors start while the context is still under half full. So it is not running out of room; facts are getting lost in a long, noisy middle.
eli5.answer: Think of a long meeting with no notes and a pile of 40-page printouts on the table. People forget the key numbers even though the room isn't full. Fix it with a whiteboard at the front listing the key facts (a case-facts block at the top), and by throwing away the pages nobody needs (trimming tool results). A bigger table wouldn't help. Rule: put the facts that matter where the model reads best, and cut the noise around them.
options: Runner-up. A bigger window (larger context) helps when history is being cut off. The errors begin at under half full, so space isn't the problem.
Correct. Key facts kept together at the top stay where the model reads most reliably.
Correct. Cutting the 40-field results down to what's used removes the noise that buries the facts.
Summaries break the verbatim-history rule and tend to round numbers and blur dates.
Fetching again adds more noise and can't recover the order number the customer typed.

deep.premise: It is tempting to think forgetting means running out of space, so a bigger window or a summary is the fix. The stem rules that out: the errors start before the window is half full. Models read the start and end of a long context best and can miss things in the middle (lost in the middle). Repeated 40-field tool results make that middle noisier.

questions.question: Over eighteen months the tier-1 agent has gathered 19 tools. Next to the four core ones sit back-office tools such as issue_credit_memo, adjust_inventory and override_price, each needed in well under 1% of tickets and occasionally called when they should not be. Selection accuracy on the four core tools has fallen from 97% to 89% since the count passed about a dozen.
